rationale: A wins because it turns the launch into cleaner reporter assignments, especially the infrastructure angle: "which partner banks hold the consumer deposits, how balances are swept, and what the consumer-facing disclosure looks like." B has good bones, but it sells facts it does not have with "What the SVB windfall became" and "the alternative that absorbed startup deposits" when the update only says Mercury became well known after SVB. A still needs a haircut on "now wants your paycheck," but its proof gates are tighter and the kept angles separate more cleanly.
gaps_in_A: "now wants your paycheck" implies payroll or direct-deposit intent that the update does not supply. Cute headline, loose fact.

"The prevailing belief on this beat is that consumer neobanking is a customer-acquisition money pit" imports outside market context without evidence in the update. It can be a real angle, but not yet a grounded one.

"the first time the SVB-era customer base is being asked to bring their personal money too" assumes existing business customers are the consumer target. The set later asks for proof, but the angle body already spent the assumption.
"same arrangement that has been the live question in fintech-banking supervision" gestures at a regulatory peg without one being supplied. It is safer as background, not as implied news heat.
gaps_in_B: "What the SVB windfall became" is the big offense. No windfall, deposit influx, or post-SVB customer split was supplied.
"the alternative that absorbed startup deposits" goes beyond "became well known as a startup-banking alternative." That is exactly how a useful follow-up angle turns into unsupported lore.
"founders and employees who already bank at those 200,000 companies" is muddled and ungrounded. The companies bank with Mercury; the employees do not necessarily do anything with Mercury.
"who is now squeezed from a new direction" claims competitor impact before proving any feature, price, yield, or segment advantage. That is launch-story helium.
